note: Shared glossary for AI Safety from Scratch and Security from Scratch. Each term has a stable id; `sites` lists which sites use it.

terms.short: Computer systems that do tasks we usually call “smart”, such as recognising speech or writing text.
AI that creates new text, images, audio or video.
Realistic fake video, image or audio of a real person, made with AI.
An AI copy of a person’s voice, made from a short recording.
A message that pretends to come from someone trusted to trick you into clicking, paying or giving away details.
A secret word or phrase agreed in advance so family members can prove who they are on the phone.
Hanging up and calling the person or company back on a number you already know is real.
A trick that talks an AI out of its safety rules, for example through role-play or a disguised request.
Instructions hidden in something the AI reads for you, such as a web page, file or email, rather than typed by you.
Giving a person or program only the access it needs, for only as long as it needs it.
Simon Willison’s name for an AI agent that has private data, reads untrusted content and can send data out: together they let an attacker steal data.
An open standard for connecting AI apps to tools and data, through small programs called MCP servers.
A design where a person must approve certain actions before the AI or agent carries them out.
A list of the only people, shops or addresses something is allowed to deal with. Everything else is blocked.
A hard limit on how much can be spent, per payment or per day, that the agent cannot raise itself.
To take back a permission you gave earlier, so it stops working.
A trick to get your money, your details or control of your accounts, usually by pretending to be someone you trust.
Faking the number or name that appears on your phone, or the sender of a message, so it looks like someone trusted.
Phishing by text message (SMS): a fake text that tries to make you tap a link, call a number or share details.
Phishing by phone call: a caller pretends to be your bank, the police or support to trick you.
A call that plays a recorded message instead of a real person talking, often asking you to press a key.
Letting another person control your phone or computer from far away through an app. Never allow it for someone who called you.
A safe app that creates, stores and fills in your passwords, so each account can have a different one.
A password made of several random words, which makes it long but easy to type.
When a company’s customer data, such as emails or passwords, is stolen or exposed.
Signing in with your password plus a second proof, such as a code or a tap on your phone.
A way to sign in with your phone’s fingerprint, face or screen lock instead of a password.
Words or a button in a message or web page that open a website when you tap them.
The real name of a website, such as twint.ch. It is the part just before the first single slash.
The small lock next to a web address. It means the connection is private, not that the website is honest.
A saved shortcut to a website you trust, so you can open it without searching or tapping links.
A square pattern you scan with your phone’s camera to open a link. A fake one can lead to a fake website.
A file sent with an email or message, such as a document or a picture.
The number or name your phone shows for an incoming call. It can be faked.
